difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — mentally unfolding a four-layer fold needs several linked ideas (mirror images across two creases, telling creases from free edges, and merging pieces that touch a crease) with a likely counting trap; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Folding and unfolding a multi-layer sheet with strips cut away: counting separate pieces from which edges of each region are creases.
stem:
A square sheet of paper occupies the region $0 \le x \le 8$, $0 \le y \le 8$ in a fixed plane (all lengths in cm). It is folded twice.

1. **First fold:** along the line $x = 4$, so that the part with $x \ge 4$ is laid over the part with $x \le 4$.
2. **Second fold:** along the line $y = 4$, so that the part of the folded sheet with $y \ge 4$ is laid over the part with $y \le 4$.

The folded sheet now occupies the square $0 \le x \le 4$, $0 \le y \le 4$ in four layers. Holding all four layers together, the paper lying in each of the following two strips of the folded sheet is cut away completely:

- Strip I: $2.5 \le x + y \le 3$
- Strip II: $4.5 \le x + y \le 5$

The sheet is then unfolded completely. Paper that is joined along a crease counts as a single piece.

The number of separate pieces of paper in the unfolded sheet is

solution.quick: In the folded square the strips leave three regions: a corner triangle at the origin ($x+y<2.5$), a middle band ($3<x+y<4.5$) and a triangle at $(4,4)$ ($x+y>5$). The corner at the origin touches only free edges, so its four layers stay separate (4 pieces). The triangle at $(4,4)$ lies on both creases and joins into one diamond, and the band meets both creases and joins into one ring. Total $4+1+1=6$.

steps.title: Regions of the folded sheet
steps.body: The lines $x+y=2.5,\,3,\,4.5,\,5$ are parallel diagonals of the folded square $[0,4]\times[0,4]$. Strip I runs from the left edge to the bottom edge, and strip II from the top edge to the right edge. Removing them leaves three regions: $T$: $x+y<2.5$ (a triangle with legs $2.5$ at the origin); $B$: $3<x+y<4.5$ (a band); $C$: $x+y>5$ (the triangle with vertices $(1,4)$, $(4,1)$, $(4,4)$).

steps.title: Creases versus free edges
steps.body: In the folded sheet the edges $x=0$ and $y=0$ are original free edges of the paper, while the edges $x=4$ and $y=4$ are creases: the paper continues across them into the other layers. On unfolding, a region that touches a crease is joined to its mirror image across that crease; a region that touches no crease is not joined to anything.

steps.title: Region $T$
steps.body: $T$ touches only the free edges $x=0$ and $y=0$ (its third side is strip I). Its four layers are the four corners of the original sheet, so they remain four separate right triangles with legs $2.5$ cm: **4 pieces**.

steps.title: Regions $C$ and $B$
steps.body: $C$ has two sides on the creases ($x=4$ from $y=1$ to $4$, and $y=4$ from $x=1$ to $4$). Mirroring across both creases joins its four copies around the centre $(4,4)$ into the single diamond $|x-4|+|y-4|\le 3$: **1 piece**. $B$ meets crease $x=4$ for $0\le y<0.5$ and crease $y=4$ for $0\le x<0.5$, so its four copies are also chained together, forming a closed ring around the diamond: **1 piece**.

steps.title: Count and check
steps.body: Pieces: $4+1+1=6$. Area check: the corner triangles have area $4\times 3.125=12.5$, the diamond $18$ and the ring $4\times 5.375=21.5$, a total of $52$; the cut-away strips remove $4\times(1.375+1.625)=12$, and $52+12=64=8^2$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $3$ is the number of regions in the folded sheet ($T$, $B$ and $C$). Unfolding mirrors the regions into the other layers, so the count changes.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $5$ is what strip I alone would give: the four corner triangles and one large remaining piece. Strip II closes into a diamond-shaped ring on unfolding and detaches the centre piece, which adds one more piece.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Four corner triangles, one centre diamond and one surrounding ring give $6$ pieces.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $12$ counts every one of the three regions once per layer ($3\times4$), as if the creases were cuts. Paper is continuous across a crease, so only the corner triangles stay in four separate copies.

solution.shortcut: Classify each region of the folded sheet by the creases it touches: no crease gives $4$ pieces, one crease gives $2$, and both creases give $1$. Here $T$ gives $4$, and $B$ and $C$ give $1$ each, so $4+1+1=6$.
solution.commonTrap: Counting the regions of the folded sheet (three) or multiplying every region by four. Whether a region's copies stay apart depends on whether it touches a crease; creases are not cuts.

import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage
N = 1600
xs = (np.arange(N) + 0.5) * 8 / N
X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing='ij')
xf = np.where(X <= 4, X, 8 - X)   # fold 1 about x=4
yf = np.where(Y <= 4, Y, 8 - Y)   # fold 2 about y=4
s = xf + yf                       # x+y evaluated in the folded sheet
S1 = (s >= 2.5) & (s <= 3)
S2 = (s >= 4.5) & (s <= 5)
n = ndimage.label(~(S1 | S2))[1]
print(n)
assert n == 6
assert ndimage.label(~S1)[1] == 5            # strip I alone: 5 pieces
crease = (abs(X - 4) < 0.02) | (abs(Y - 4) < 0.02)
assert ndimage.label(~(S1 | S2 | crease))[1] == 12   # creases wrongly treated as cuts

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — each sentence must be tested against a different rule (inverted conditional, mandative subjunctive, comparative for two items, verb pattern after 'suggest'), and three correct sentences contain constructions that look wrong at first sight; about 2 minutes.
concept: Spotting the ungrammatical sentence: verb patterns after 'suggest' versus inverted conditionals, mandative subjunctive and the comparative for two items.
stem: Exactly one of the following four sentences is **not** grammatically correct. Select that sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Had the surveyors verified the plot boundaries before construction began, the long dispute with the neighbouring landowner would never have arisen.

options.label: B
options.text: The regulations require that every contractor who handles hazardous material carry a valid licence at all times.

options.label: C
options.text: Of the two vendors that bid for the contract, the second offered the more flexible payment terms.

options.label: D
options.text: After reviewing the inspection logs, the auditor suggested the firm to revise its safety procedures before the next audit.

solution.quick: Sentences A, B and C use correct formal constructions: an inverted third conditional, the mandative subjunctive (base form 'carry') and a comparative with 'the more' for two items. In D, 'suggest' cannot take an object followed by a to-infinitive; it needs 'suggested that the firm revise' or 'suggested revising'.

steps.title: Test sentence A
steps.body: 'Had the surveyors verified ...' is the inverted form of 'If the surveyors had verified ...' (third conditional). The main clause 'would never have arisen' uses the matching 'would have + past participle'. Both halves agree, so A is correct.

steps.title: Test sentence B
steps.body: After verbs and nouns of requirement (require, demand, insist, recommend) a that-clause takes the base form of the verb for every subject. 'Every contractor ... carry' is the mandative subjunctive, so 'carries' is not needed. B is correct.

steps.title: Test sentence C
steps.body: When exactly two things are compared the comparative is used, with 'the' when the pair is specified by 'Of the two ...'. 'The second offered the more flexible payment terms' is therefore correct; 'most' would be wrong here.

steps.title: Test sentence D
steps.body: The reviewing phrase correctly refers to the auditor. The fault lies in 'suggested the firm to revise': 'suggest' takes a that-clause ('suggested that the firm revise') or a gerund ('suggested revising'), but not an object plus a to-infinitive. That pattern belongs to verbs such as 'advise', 'ask' or 'urge'. D is the faulty sentence.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct sentence: an inverted conditional ('Had ... verified') paired with 'would never have arisen'. It is not the faulty one.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct sentence: 'carry' is the base-form (subjunctive) verb required after 'require that'. It is not the faulty one.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct sentence: two vendors are compared, so the comparative 'the more flexible' is right. It is not the faulty one.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Faulty sentence: 'suggested the firm to revise' uses an object plus to-infinitive after 'suggest'. It should read 'suggested that the firm revise' or 'suggested revising'.

solution.shortcut: Check verb patterns first: 'suggest', 'recommend' and 'propose' take a that-clause (base form) or a gerund, never object + to-infinitive, whereas 'advise', 'ask' and 'urge' take object + to-infinitive.
solution.commonTrap: Flagging B ('carry' instead of 'carries') or C ('more' instead of 'most') because they sound unusual, and so missing the verb-pattern error in D.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one idea (weighted rates read from a table) carried through four or five routine steps: cancelled counts, target count, required Old Town count and rate; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Weighted percentage from a table: finding the rate change in one category needed to reach a target overall rate.
stem:
A ride-hailing service operates in four zones of a city. The table gives, for one week, the number of ride requests received in each zone and the percentage of those requests that were cancelled.

| Zone | Requests (thousands) | Cancelled (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Harbour | 250 | 12 |
| Old Town | 150 | 20 |
| Tech Park | 400 | 5 |
| Airport | 200 | 10 |

The city-wide cancellation rate is the total number of cancelled requests expressed as a percentage of the total number of requests. The service wants the city-wide cancellation rate to be exactly $8\%$ next week. It expects the number of requests in every zone to stay the same and the cancellation rates of Harbour, Tech Park and Airport to stay unchanged, so that the whole improvement has to come from Old Town.

By how many percentage points (rounded off to one decimal place) must the cancellation rate of Old Town fall?

solution.quick: Total requests are $1000$ thousand, and $8\%$ of them is $80$ thousand cancellations. The other three zones already contribute $30+20+20=70$ thousand, so Old Town may have only $10$ thousand cancellations out of $150$ thousand, a rate of $6.67\%$. The fall is $20-6.67\approx 13.3$ percentage points.

steps.title: Cancelled requests this week
steps.body: Cancelled (in thousands): Harbour $250\times0.12=30$; Old Town $150\times0.20=30$; Tech Park $400\times0.05=20$; Airport $200\times0.10=20$. Total requests $=250+150+400+200=1000$ thousand and total cancellations $=100$ thousand, so the current city-wide rate is $10\%$.

steps.title: Target number of cancellations
steps.body: A city-wide rate of $8\%$ on an unchanged $1000$ thousand requests allows $0.08\times1000=80$ thousand cancellations.

steps.title: Old Town's allowance
steps.body: Harbour, Tech Park and Airport still contribute $30+20+20=70$ thousand, so Old Town may contribute only $80-70=10$ thousand cancellations out of its $150$ thousand requests. Its new rate is $\dfrac{10}{150}\times100=6.67\%$.

steps.title: Fall in percentage points
steps.body: Fall $=20-6.67=13.33\approx13.3$ percentage points. Check: new total $=70+10=80$ thousand, which is $8\%$ of $1000$ thousand.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $2.0$ is the fall in the city-wide rate ($10\%$ to $8\%$). Old Town holds only $15\%$ of all requests, so a $2$-point city-wide fall needs a much larger fall in Old Town's own rate.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $6.7$ is Old Town's new cancellation rate, not the fall from its present $20\%$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: A fall of $13.33$ points takes Old Town to $6.67\%$ and the city-wide rate to exactly $8\%$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $20.0$ confuses units: $20$ thousand fewer cancellations is $20\%$ of the $100$ thousand now cancelled, but that is a relative cut in the total, not a fall in Old Town's rate in percentage points.

solution.shortcut: Old Town carries $150/1000=15\%$ of all requests, so each point off its rate lowers the city-wide rate by $0.15$ points. A $2$-point city-wide fall therefore needs $2/0.15\approx13.3$ points.
solution.commonTrap: Reporting the new Old Town rate ($6.7$) instead of the fall, or applying the city-wide change of $2$ points directly to Old Town without weighting by its share of requests.

req  = {'Harbour': 250, 'Old Town': 150, 'Tech Park': 400, 'Airport': 200}   # thousands
rate = {'Harbour': 12, 'Old Town': 20, 'Tech Park': 5, 'Airport': 10}          # % cancelled
canc = {z: req[z] * rate[z] / 100 for z in req}
R, C = sum(req.values()), sum(canc.values())
print(R, C, C / R * 100)
need_old = 0.08 * R - (C - canc['Old Town'])       # cancellations Old Town may keep
new_rate = need_old / req['Old Town'] * 100
fall = rate['Old Town'] - new_rate
print(need_old, new_rate, fall)
assert round(fall, 1) == 13.3
# distractors: 2.0 (city-wide fall), 6.7 (new rate), 20.0 (relative cut in total cancellations)
print(C / R * 100 - 8, new_rate, (C - 0.08 * R) / C * 100)

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (linear independence in a function space) needing three routine identity checks and one short independence argument; about 1.5 minutes.
concept: Linear dependence and independence in a vector space of functions: hidden linear relations from angle-addition, double-angle and hyperbolic identities.
stem:
Consider the real vector space of all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. Exactly one of the following sets of functions is linearly independent. Which one is it?

(Recall that $\cosh x = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)$.)

solution.quick: Sets A, C and D each hide a linear relation: $\sin(x+\pi/6)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x+\tfrac12\cos x$, $\cos^2x=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cos2x$ and $\cosh x=\tfrac12e^x+\tfrac12e^{-x}$. For $\{\sin x,\sin2x,\sin3x\}$, substituting $x=\pi/2,\ \pi/4,\ \pi/6$ in $a\sin x+b\sin2x+c\sin3x=0$ forces $a=b=c=0$, so only B is independent.

steps.title: Set A is dependent
steps.body: By the angle-addition formula, $\sin(x+\pi/6)=\sin x\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+\cos x\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x+\frac12\cos x$. The third function is a linear combination of the first two.

steps.title: Sets C and D are dependent
steps.body: For C, $\cos2x=2\cos^2x-1$, so $1\cdot 1+1\cdot\cos2x-2\cdot\cos^2x=0$ for all $x$, a non-trivial relation. For D, $\cosh x=\tfrac12e^{x}+\tfrac12e^{-x}$, so $\cosh x-\tfrac12e^{x}-\tfrac12e^{-x}=0$.

steps.title: Set B is independent
steps.body: Suppose $a\sin x+b\sin2x+c\sin3x=0$ for every $x$. At $x=\pi/2$: $a-c=0$, so $c=a$. At $x=\pi/4$: $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}a+b+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}c=0$, which with $c=a$ gives $b=-\sqrt2\,a$. At $x=\pi/6$: $\frac12a+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}b+c=0$, which with $c=a$ gives $b=-\sqrt3\,a$. Then $\sqrt2\,a=\sqrt3\,a$, so $a=0$, hence $b=c=0$. Only the trivial combination vanishes.

steps.title: Check and conclude
steps.body: The Wronskian of $\sin x,\sin2x,\sin3x$ at $x=\pi/2$ is $\det\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\0&-2&0\\-1&0&9\end{bmatrix}=-16\neq0$, which confirms independence. The independent set is B.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Dependent: $\sin(x+\pi/6)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x+\frac12\cos x$, so the third function lies in the span of the first two.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Independent: the only solution of $a\sin x+b\sin2x+c\sin3x=0$ for all $x$ is $a=b=c=0$. The triple-angle identity $\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$ is not a linear relation among $\sin x$, $\sin2x$ and $\sin3x$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Dependent: $1+\cos2x-2\cos^2x=0$ for all $x$ (double-angle identity).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Dependent: $\cosh x=\frac12e^{x}+\frac12e^{-x}$, so $\cosh x$ is a combination of the other two functions.

solution.shortcut: Sines of different integer frequencies are mutually orthogonal on $[0,2\pi]$, hence independent. For the other sets, look for a hidden identity (angle addition, double angle, definition of $\cosh$).
solution.commonTrap: Choosing A, C or D because the functions look different. Linear dependence in a function space must hold for every $x$, and trigonometric and hyperbolic identities often supply a hidden linear relation. Rejecting B because of the triple-angle identity is also wrong, since that identity is not linear in $\sin x$.

import numpy as np, sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
sets = {
 'A': [sp.sin(x), sp.cos(x), sp.sin(x + sp.pi/6)],
 'B': [sp.sin(x), sp.sin(2*x), sp.sin(3*x)],
 'C': [sp.Integer(1), sp.cos(2*x), sp.cos(x)**2],
 'D': [sp.exp(x), sp.exp(-x), sp.cosh(x)],
}
pts = np.linspace(0.1, 6.0, 40)
rank = {}
for k, fs in sets.items():
    M = np.array([[float(sp.N(f.subs(x, p))) for p in pts] for f in fs])
    rank[k] = np.linalg.matrix_rank(M, tol=1e-9)
print(rank)
assert [k for k, r in rank.items() if r == 3] == ['B']
# exact dependence relations for A, C, D
assert sp.simplify(sp.expand_trig(sp.sin(x + sp.pi/6)) - (sp.sqrt(3)/2*sp.sin(x) + sp.cos(x)/2)) == 0
assert sp.simplify(sp.cos(x)**2 - sp.Rational(1, 2) - sp.cos(2*x)/2) == 0
assert sp.simplify(sp.cosh(x).rewrite(sp.exp) - (sp.exp(x) + sp.exp(-x))/2) == 0
# Wronskian of set B at pi/2
W = sp.Matrix([[sp.diff(f, x, i) for f in sets['B']] for i in range(3)]).det()
print(sp.N(W.subs(x, sp.pi/2)))
assert abs(sp.N(W.subs(x, sp.pi/2)) + 16) < 1e-9

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (sample space and event algebra) with four short checks, each of which needs the list of the eight equally likely outcomes; about 2 minutes.
concept: Sample space and event algebra: exhaustive versus mutually exclusive events, and why a coarser sample space need not be equally likely.
stem:
Three members of a club, $P$, $Q$ and $R$, each sign up independently for exactly one of two workshops, $G$ or $H$, and each member is equally likely to choose either workshop. The outcome of the experiment is recorded as the triple of workshops chosen by $(P, Q, R)$; for example, $GHG$ means that $P$ and $R$ chose $G$ and $Q$ chose $H$. Let $S$ be the sample space of these triples, and let $N$ be the number of members who choose $G$. Define the events

- $E_1$: $N \ge 1$,
- $E_2$: $N \le 1$,
- $E_3$: $N$ is even (zero counts as even),
- $E_4$: member $P$ chooses $H$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: $E_1$ and $E_2$ are collectively exhaustive (that is, $E_1\cup E_2=S$) but are not mutually exclusive.

options.label: C
options.text: If the outcome were recorded only as the value of $N$, the sample space would be $\{0,1,2,3\}$ and its four outcomes would be equally likely.

options.label: D
options.text: The event $E_4^{c}\cap E_3$ contains exactly two outcomes of $S$.

solution.quick: List the $8$ equally likely triples by $N$: $N=0$: $HHH$; $N=1$: $GHH,HGH,HHG$; $N=2$: $GGH,GHG,HGG$; $N=3$: $GGG$. Then $E_1\cup E_2=S$ with $E_1\cap E_2=\{N=1\}\ne\varnothing$ (A true); $E_2\cap E_3=\{HHH\}$ (B false); the values of $N$ have probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$ (C false); $E_4^c\cap E_3=\{GGH,GHG\}$ (D true).

steps.title: Sample space and the events
steps.body: Each of the $2^3=8$ triples has probability $\tfrac18$. By the value of $N$: $N=0$: $\{HHH\}$; $N=1$: $\{GHH,HGH,HHG\}$; $N=2$: $\{GGH,GHG,HGG\}$; $N=3$: $\{GGG\}$. Hence $E_1=\{N\in\{1,2,3\}\}$ has $7$ outcomes, $E_2=\{N\in\{0,1\}\}$ has $4$, $E_3=\{N\in\{0,2\}\}$ has $4$, and $E_4=\{HGG,HGH,HHG,HHH\}$.

steps.title: Statement A
steps.body: Every value of $N$ is either $\ge1$ or $\le1$, so $E_1\cup E_2=S$. Their intersection is $\{N=1\}=\{GHH,HGH,HHG\}\neq\varnothing$, so they are not mutually exclusive. **True.**

steps.title: Statements B and C
steps.body: $E_2\cap E_3=\{N=0\}=\{HHH\}\ne\varnothing$, because zero is even and at most one, so B is **false**. Recording only $N$ gives the sample space $\{0,1,2,3\}$ with probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$, which are not equal, so C is **false**.

steps.title: Statement D
steps.body: $E_4^c$ is the event that $P$ chooses $G$: $\{GGG,GGH,GHG,GHH\}$. Among these, $N$ is even only for $GGH$ and $GHG$ ($N=2$); $GGG$ has $N=3$ and $GHH$ has $N=1$. So $E_4^c\cap E_3=\{GGH,GHG\}$ has exactly two outcomes. **True.**

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct: $E_1\cup E_2=S$, and $E_1\cap E_2=\{GHH,HGH,HHG\}$ is non-empty.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect: both events contain the outcome $HHH$ (zero members choose $G$, which is even and at most one).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect: the coarser outcomes $0,1,2,3$ have probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$, so they are not equally likely.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct: $E_4^c\cap E_3=\{GGH,GHG\}$.

solution.commonTrap: Treating the values of $N$ as equally likely outcomes (a coarser sample space is generally not equiprobable), or overlooking that $0$ is even, which puts $HHH$ in both $E_2$ and $E_3$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — a non-routine critical point (where the derivative does not exist) must be found alongside the stationary point, then a sign analysis and a fractional-power evaluation are needed; solving only $f'(x)=0$ is a likely trap; about 3 minutes.
concept: Local extrema at a cusp: critical points include points where the derivative does not exist, classified by the first-derivative sign change.
stem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by

$$f(x) = (x-10)\,x^{2/3},$$

where $x^{2/3}=\left(\sqrt[3]{x}\right)^{2}$ for every real $x$. The function $f$ has exactly one local maximum and exactly one local minimum. The local maximum value of $f$ exceeds the local minimum value of $f$ by ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).

solution.quick: For $x\ne0$, $f'(x)=\dfrac{5x-20}{3\,x^{1/3}}$, which vanishes at $x=4$ and does not exist at $x=0$ (a cusp). The sign of $f'$ is $+,-,+$ on $(-\infty,0)$, $(0,4)$, $(4,\infty)$, so $x=0$ is a local maximum ($f=0$) and $x=4$ is a local minimum ($f=-6\cdot4^{2/3}\approx-15.119$). The difference is $15.12$.

steps.title: Derivative
steps.body: For $x\neq0$: $f'(x)=x^{2/3}+\tfrac23(x-10)x^{-1/3}=x^{-1/3}\left[x+\tfrac{2}{3}(x-10)\right]=\dfrac{5x-20}{3\,x^{1/3}}$. As $x\to0$, $|f'(x)|\to\infty$, so $f$ is continuous at $0$ but not differentiable there.

steps.title: Critical points
steps.body: $f'(x)=0$ gives $5x-20=0$, that is $x=4$. In addition, $x=0$ is a critical point because $f'(0)$ does not exist although $f(0)$ is defined.

steps.title: Sign of $f'$
steps.body: For $x<0$: numerator $5x-20<0$ and $x^{1/3}<0$, so $f'>0$. For $0<x<4$: numerator $<0$, denominator $>0$, so $f'<0$. For $x>4$: both are positive, so $f'>0$. Thus $f$ rises, then falls, then rises: $x=0$ is a local maximum (a cusp) and $x=4$ is a local minimum.

steps.title: Values and difference
steps.body: $f(0)=0$. $f(4)=(4-10)\cdot4^{2/3}=-6\cdot2^{4/3}=-6\times2.5198\approx-15.119$. The local maximum value minus the local minimum value is $0-(-15.119)=15.119\approx15.12$.

solution.commonTrap: Solving only $f'(x)=0$. That finds the minimum at $x=4$ but misses the cusp at $x=0$, where $f'$ does not exist and which is the local maximum. The second-derivative test cannot be used at $x=0$.

import numpy as np
f = lambda t: np.cbrt(t)**2 * (t - 10)          # x^(2/3) = (cube root of x)^2
d = lambda t: (5*t - 20) / (3*np.cbrt(t))        # f'(x) for x != 0
print([np.sign(d(t)) for t in (-1, 1, 3, 5)])    # + - - +  -> local max at 0, local min at 4
t = np.linspace(-20, 40, 600001); y = f(t)
mx = t[1:-1][(y[1:-1] > y[:-2]) & (y[1:-1] > y[2:])]
mn = t[1:-1][(y[1:-1] < y[:-2]) & (y[1:-1] < y[2:])]
print(mx, mn)
assert len(mx) == 1 and abs(mx[0]) < 1e-3 and len(mn) == 1 and abs(mn[0] - 4) < 1e-3
ans = f(0.0) - f(4.0)
print(ans)
assert round(ans, 2) == 15.12

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (prediction and residual from a fitted multiple regression equation) in a single substitution; about 1 minute.
concept: Prediction and residual (observed minus fitted) from a fitted multiple linear regression equation.
stem:
A data-centre engineer fits the multiple linear regression model

$$\hat{y} = 4.2 + 0.35\,x_1 + 1.8\,x_2 - 0.6\,x_3,$$

where $\hat{y}$ is the predicted power draw of a server rack (in kW), $x_1$ is the average CPU utilisation (in %), $x_2$ is the number of GPUs installed in the rack and $x_3$ is the coolant flow rate (in litres per second). A rack with $x_1=60$, $x_2=4$ and $x_3=5$ actually draws $31.0$ kW.

The residual $y-\hat{y}$ for this rack, in kW, is

solution.quick: The fitted value is $\hat y=4.2+0.35(60)+1.8(4)-0.6(5)=4.2+21+7.2-3=29.4$ kW. The residual is observed minus fitted: $31.0-29.4=1.6$ kW.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: The residual of an observation is $e=y-\hat{y}$: the observed value minus the value fitted by the regression equation.

steps.title: Fitted value
steps.body: Substitute the rack's values: $0.35\times60=21$, $1.8\times4=7.2$ and $-0.6\times5=-3.0$. Then $\hat{y}=4.2+21+7.2-3.0=29.4$ kW.

steps.title: Residual
steps.body: $e=y-\hat{y}=31.0-29.4=1.6$ kW. The residual is positive, so the model underestimates this rack's power draw.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: This has the sign reversed ($\hat y-y$). The residual is observed minus fitted, so it is $+1.6$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: This drops the intercept: $\hat y=21+7.2-3=25.2$ and $31.0-25.2=5.8$. The intercept $4.2$ must be included.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This adds the $x_3$ term instead of subtracting it: $\hat y=4.2+21+7.2+3=35.4$ and $31.0-35.4=-4.4$. The coefficient of $x_3$ is negative.

solution.commonTrap: Reversing the sign of the residual (using $\hat y-y$), forgetting the intercept, or ignoring the negative coefficient of $x_3$.

answerVerification.checkCode:
b0, b1, b2, b3 = 4.2, 0.35, 1.8, -0.6
x1, x2, x3, y = 60, 4, 5, 31.0
yhat = b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2 + b3*x3
resid = y - yhat
print(yhat, resid)
assert abs(yhat - 29.4) < 1e-9 and abs(resid - 1.6) < 1e-9
# distractors: reversed sign, no intercept, wrong sign on the x3 term
print(-resid, y - (b1*x1 + b2*x2 + b3*x3), y - (b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2 - b3*x3))

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — an MSQ whose four statements each need their own computation (event independence, full-table independence, conditioning on a complement, equality of two reversed conditionals), with a likely trap in generalising from one independent pair; about 3 minutes.
concept: Marginal, conditional and joint probabilities from a two-way table: independence of events versus independence of random variables, and reversed conditionals.
stem:
A coding-contest platform logged $200$ submissions. Each submission is classified by the programming language used and by the verdict it received. The counts are as follows.

| Language | Accepted | Wrong answer | Time limit exceeded |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 50 | 30 | 20 |
| C++ | 40 | 20 | 10 |
| Java | 10 | 10 | 10 |

One of the $200$ logged submissions is chosen uniformly at random. Let $L$ be its language and $V$ its verdict.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The events $\{L=\text{Python}\}$ and $\{V=\text{Time limit exceeded}\}$ are independent.

options.label: B
options.text: The random variables $L$ and $V$ are independent.

solution.quick: The marginals are $P(\text{Python})=0.5$, $P(\text{C++})=0.35$, $P(\text{Java})=0.15$ and $P(\text{Acc})=0.5$, $P(\text{WA})=0.3$, $P(\text{TLE})=0.2$. A holds ($0.10=0.5\times0.2$); B fails in the cell (C++, TLE): $0.05\ne0.35\times0.2=0.07$; C holds ($20/100$); D holds (both sides equal $0.5$).

steps.title: Marginals
steps.body: Row totals: Python $100$, C++ $70$, Java $30$. Column totals: Accepted $100$, Wrong answer $60$, Time limit exceeded $40$. So $P(\text{Python})=0.5$, $P(\text{C++})=0.35$, $P(\text{Java})=0.15$, and $P(\text{Acc})=0.5$, $P(\text{WA})=0.3$, $P(\text{TLE})=0.2$.

steps.title: Statement A
steps.body: $P(\text{Python}\cap\text{TLE})=\dfrac{20}{200}=0.10$ and $P(\text{Python})\,P(\text{TLE})=0.5\times0.2=0.10$. The two events are independent. **True.**

steps.title: Statement B
steps.body: Independence of $L$ and $V$ requires every cell to equal the product of its marginals. For (C++, TLE): $P=\dfrac{10}{200}=0.05$, but $P(\text{C++})P(\text{TLE})=0.35\times0.2=0.07$. So $L$ and $V$ are not independent (the row proportions differ: Python $0.5,0.3,0.2$; C++ $\tfrac47,\tfrac27,\tfrac17$; Java $\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13$). **False.**

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: C: $V\ne\text{Accepted}$ covers $60+40=100$ submissions, of which the Java ones number $10+10=20$, so the probability is $20/100=0.2$. **True.** D: $P(\text{Python}\mid\text{Acc})=\dfrac{50}{100}=0.5$ and $P(\text{Acc}\mid\text{Python})=\dfrac{50}{100}=0.5$. They are equal because $P(\text{Python})=P(\text{Acc})=0.5$ (from $P(A\mid B)P(B)=P(A\cap B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)$). **True.**

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct: $P(\text{Python}\cap\text{TLE})=0.10=0.5\times0.2$, so these two events are independent.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect: independence of random variables must hold in every cell. For (C++, TLE), $0.05\ne0.35\times0.2=0.07$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct: $60+40=100$ submissions have a verdict other than Accepted, and $10+10=20$ of them are Java, giving $0.2$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct: both conditional probabilities equal $50/100=0.5$, because $P(\text{Python})=P(\text{Accepted})=0.5$.

solution.commonTrap: Concluding that $L$ and $V$ are independent because one pair of events, (Python, TLE), is independent. Independence of random variables needs every cell of the table to match the product of its marginals.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
T = np.array([[50, 30, 20],      # Python: Accepted, Wrong answer, TLE
              [40, 20, 10],      # C++
              [10, 10, 10]], dtype=float)   # Java
J = T / T.sum()
pL, pV = J.sum(1), J.sum(0)
A = np.isclose(J[0, 2], pL[0] * pV[2])                       # {Python} indep {TLE}
B = np.allclose(J, np.outer(pL, pV))                          # L, V independent (all cells)
C = np.isclose(T[2, 1:].sum() / T[:, 1:].sum(), 0.2)          # P(Java | V != Accepted)
D = np.isclose(T[0, 0] / T[:, 0].sum(), T[0, 0] / T[0].sum()) # P(Py|Acc) = P(Acc|Py)
print(A, B, C, D, J[1, 2], pL[1] * pV[2])
assert (A, B, C, D) == (True, False, True, True)

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — two linked ideas (recover the missing frequency from the total, then interpolate within a median class of unequal width) with routine arithmetic; about 2 minutes.
concept: Median of grouped data with unequal class widths: cumulative frequency and linear interpolation within the median class.
stem:
A hospital pharmacy recorded the waiting time $t$ (in minutes) of $100$ patients. The data are grouped into classes of unequal width, and the frequency of the class $30\le t<50$ is not shown.

| Waiting time $t$ (minutes) | Number of patients |
|---|---|
| $0\le t<10$ | 10 |
| $10\le t<20$ | 15 |
| $20\le t<30$ | 20 |
| $30\le t<50$ | not shown |
| $50\le t<80$ | 20 |

Assume that the waiting times are spread uniformly within each class, and estimate the median waiting time by linear interpolation within the median class.

The estimated median, in minutes, rounded off to two decimal places, is ________.

solution.quick: The missing frequency is $100-(10+15+20+20)=35$. The cumulative frequencies are $10,25,45,80,100$, so the median (the $50$th value) lies in $30\le t<50$. Median $=30+\dfrac{50-45}{35}\times20=30+2.857\approx32.86$ minutes.

steps.title: Missing frequency
steps.body: The frequencies must add up to $100$, so the class $30\le t<50$ holds $100-(10+15+20+20)=35$ patients.

steps.title: Median class
steps.body: Cumulative frequencies: $10,\ 25,\ 45$ (up to $t=30$), $80$ (up to $t=50$) and $100$. The median is at position $n/2=50$. Since $45<50\le80$, the median class is $30\le t<50$, with lower limit $L=30$, class width $h=20$ and frequency $f=35$.

steps.title: Linear interpolation
steps.body: $\text{Median}=L+\dfrac{n/2-F}{f}\,h=30+\dfrac{50-45}{35}\times20$, where $F=45$ is the cumulative frequency before the class. This gives $30+\dfrac{100}{35}=30+2.857=32.857$.

steps.title: Round
steps.body: The estimated median is $32.857\approx32.86$ minutes.

solution.commonTrap: Using only the $65$ patients whose frequencies are shown, so that $n/2=32.5$ falls in the wrong class (giving $23.75$), or interpolating with the width $10$ of the earlier classes instead of the median class width $20$ (giving $31.43$).

answerVerification.checkCode:
edges = [0, 10, 20, 30, 50, 80]
freq = [10, 15, 20, None, 20]
n = 100
freq[3] = n - sum(f for f in freq if f is not None)       # missing class frequency
cum = 0
for lo, hi, f in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:], freq):
    if cum + f >= n / 2:
        med = lo + (n / 2 - cum) / f * (hi - lo)         # interpolate in the median class
        break
    cum += f
print(freq, lo, hi, cum, med)
assert freq[3] == 35 and round(med, 2) == 32.86
# trap values: n=65 with wrong class, and width 10 instead of 20
print(20 + (65 / 2 - 25) / 20 * 10, 30 + (n / 2 - 45) / 35 * 10)
